analysis.one_liner: Gives teaching and research assistants at private colleges federal collective bargaining rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote; it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal labor law so that graduate students who work as teaching or research assistants at private universities count as employees under the National Labor Relations Act. That would let them form unions and bargain over pay and working conditions, no matter whether their work is tied to their studies. It would not cover students at public universities, which are governed by state law. The bill was introduced in April 2008, sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Teaching and research assistants at private colleges and universities, who would gain the legal right to organize and bargain collectively over wages, hours, and working conditions. Unions representing them would gain new members and bargaining rights.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds graduate students who perform work for pay at a private university's direction to the NLRA's definition of 'employee,' whether or not the work relates to their courses of study [S2] [S3].
That change would give these assistants, who are currently excluded from federal labor law protections, the right to form unions and bargain with their universities [S2].
The bill covers only students at private institutions of higher education, since public universities are treated differently under the NLRA [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private universities would bear the cost: they would have to recognize and bargain with assistant unions, and labor costs for teaching and research work could rise. Some of that cost could be passed on through tuition or reduced assistantships.

drawbacks.text: Universities have long argued that graduate teaching and research work is part of academic training rather than ordinary employment, and that treating students as employees could entangle union bargaining in academic decisions about coursework and research assignments — exactly the line the bill erases, since it covers the work 'whether or not the work relates to the student's course of study' [S3].

The bill would raise labor costs at private universities for assistant work, which institutions could absorb through tuition, stipends, or fewer assistantship positions — costs that land partly on students themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: a large group of low-paid workers, excluded from federal labor protections since a 2004 labor board ruling treated them as students rather than employees, would gain a genuine legal right to bargain. The costs are real but narrower — administrative friction at universities and possible pressure on tuition or assistantship funding. The bill was a single-section amendment with no offsetting benefits for universities, so it was essentially a one-side transfer of bargaining power to the assistants.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee in April 2008, and the committee never acted on it; it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the bill on April 17, 2008, joined by Reps. Grijalva, Tierney, and Andrews [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day, and no further action was taken in the House [S5].
The bill attracted 17 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any Senate action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private university administrations are better off, because they continue to set teaching and research assistant pay and conditions without a federal duty to recognize or bargain with assistant unions. Graduate assistants remain outside federal labor law, leaving them no collective bargaining rights.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 supporters on record — the sponsor plus 17 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican supported the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have required private institutions to recognize teaching and research assistant unions and bargain over pay and conditions, a direct cost and loss of unilateral control over assistant labor. The industry's interest in this bill ran against the assistants who do much of the teaching and research work.
Unions would gain the ability to organize tens of thousands of graduate assistants at private universities, expanding membership and bargaining coverage.
